tips.title: Two questions sort all three
tips.body: Ask **what moves** and **which way**. Water through a partially permeable membrane, down the gradient → **osmosis**. Anything else down the gradient → **diffusion**. **Against** the gradient → **active transport**, and that is the only one needing **energy from respiration**.

tips.title: Only active transport needs energy
tips.body: Diffusion and osmosis are **passive**: the particles are moving anyway, and the gradient does the work. **Active transport** pushes substances the wrong way, so it needs **energy from respiration** and **carrier proteins**. A cell doing a lot of it has **many mitochondria** — a giveaway in an unfamiliar question.

tips.title: Osmosis is about water, always
tips.body: Osmosis moves **water**, and only water. It goes from where water is **more** concentrated — the **dilute** solution — to where it is **less** concentrated. Saying *from high to low concentration* without saying **of water** describes the solute moving the opposite way.

tips.title: Percentage change, not raw change
tips.body: $\dfrac{\text{change}}{\text{original}} \times 100$. Cylinders never start at the same mass, so a raw gain of 0.3 g means something different for a 2 g piece than for a 6 g one. The percentage is what makes them comparable — and it keeps its **sign**: a loss is **negative**.

tips.title: Blot before weighing
tips.body: Surface water left on a potato cylinder is weighed as though the cell had absorbed it, so every cylinder is **blotted dry** the same way before and after. Blotting some harder than others turns a control into a source of error.

steps.title: Diffusion
steps.body:
**Diffusion is the net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration** — that is, **down a concentration gradient**.

**The word *net* is doing real work.** Particles move **randomly** in all directions all the time. They are not attracted to the empty space. It is simply that when there are more particles on one side, **more happen to wander across** that way than come back — so the **overall** movement is down the gradient, even though individual particles go both ways. Once the concentrations are equal, particles keep moving but there is **no net movement**.

**Diffusion is passive.** It needs **no energy from respiration**, because the particles were moving anyway.

**In the body:**

- **oxygen** diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, and from the blood into cells
- **carbon dioxide** diffuses the other way
- **urea** diffuses out of cells into the plasma

**What makes it faster** — the same four factors that come back in Unit 8:

- a **steeper concentration gradient**
- a **higher temperature**, giving particles more kinetic energy
- a **larger surface area**
- a **shorter distance** to travel

steps.title: Osmosis
steps.body:
**Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution, through a partially permeable membrane.**

That sentence has **three** parts and all three are marked:

1. it is **water** that moves
2. from **dilute to concentrated** — which is the same as **high water concentration to low water concentration**
3. through a **partially permeable membrane**

**Why the membrane matters.** Partially permeable means **water molecules are small enough to pass** but the **dissolved solute molecules are too large**. So the solute cannot even out by moving itself; the **water** has to move instead. Without such a membrane you would just have diffusion of the solute.

**Osmosis is passive** too. No energy from respiration is needed.

**In plant cells:**

- Water **in** → the cell swells and pushes against the cell wall → the cell is **turgid**, and the plant stands up.
- Water **out** → the cell goes **flaccid**, and if enough leaves, the membrane **pulls away from the cell wall** and the cell is **plasmolysed**. The plant wilts.

**In animal cells there is no cell wall**, so the results are more serious: too much water in and the cell **bursts (lyses)**; too much out and it **shrinks and crinkles**. That is why the water potential of blood has to be controlled so carefully.

**The confusing bit, said plainly.** A **concentrated** sugar solution has **more sugar** and therefore **less water**. Water moves **towards** it. If you find yourself saying water moves from high to low concentration, add the words **of water** and check it still says what you meant.

steps.title: Active transport
steps.body:
**Active transport is the movement of substances against a concentration gradient** — from a **lower** concentration to a **higher** one — using **energy from respiration** and **carrier proteins** in the membrane.

**It is the opposite of what would happen on its own**, which is exactly why it costs energy. Diffusion and osmosis go the way things were going anyway; active transport pushes uphill.

**The two examples the course uses:**

- **Mineral ions into root hair cells.** The soil is very **dilute** in minerals and the root hair cell already has **more** of them. Diffusion would move them **out**. Active transport brings them **in** against the gradient — which is the only reason plants can take up minerals at all.
- **Glucose absorbed from the small intestine** into the blood, and **reabsorbed in the kidney tubules**, so that no glucose is wasted even when the concentration in the gut or the filtrate is lower than in the blood.

**The giveaway in an unfamiliar question is mitochondria.** A cell that does a lot of active transport needs a lot of **energy from respiration**, so it has **many mitochondria**. Root hair cells and the cells lining the small intestine both do. If a question shows you a cell packed with mitochondria and asks what it does, active transport is a strong candidate.

**And a second giveaway: it can be stopped.** Anything that stops **respiration** — a lack of oxygen, or a poison such as cyanide — stops **active transport** but leaves diffusion and osmosis running. An experiment where one kind of uptake halts without oxygen and another continues has just distinguished the two.

steps.title: Percentage change in mass
steps.body:
**Spec point 1.17** asks for the percentage gain and loss of mass in osmosis.

$$\% \text{ change} = \frac{\text{change in mass}}{\text{original mass}} \times 100$$

**Keep the sign.** A gain is **positive**, a loss is **negative**, and the sign is what tells you which way the water went. An answer of *12%* when the potato lost mass has thrown away the finding.

steps.title: Core practical: osmosis in potatoes
steps.body:
**This is core practical 4**, and it is the one whose method questions are about **fair testing** rather than chemistry.

**The method:**

1. Cut potato cylinders with a **cork borer**, so they all have the **same diameter**, and trim them to the **same length**.
2. **Blot** each one dry and record its **starting mass**.
3. Put one cylinder into each of a range of **sucrose solutions** — say 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mol/dm³ — using the **same volume** of solution each time.
4. Leave them for the **same time**, at the **same temperature**.
5. Remove, **blot dry in the same way**, and record the **final mass**.
6. Calculate the **percentage change** for each.

**Why blotting matters.** Water clinging to the outside is weighed as though the cell had taken it in. Blotting removes it — but only if every cylinder is blotted the **same way**, which is why *blot dry* appears in the mark scheme rather than *dry them*.

**Reading the graph.** Plot **percentage change against concentration**. The line crosses **zero** where the solution is the **same concentration as the cell contents**, because there is **no net movement** of water. Above that concentration the cylinders **lose** mass; below it they **gain**.

**That crossing point is the result of the experiment.** A question asking what the graph tells you about the potato is asking you to read it off — and it is found by **where the line crosses zero**, not by the lowest or highest point.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Say *net*, and mean it.** Particles never stop moving. Diffusion ends when there is **no net movement**, not when movement ceases, and the same is true of osmosis. A cylinder whose mass does not change has water crossing its membrane in **both** directions at **equal rates** — that is a much better answer than *nothing happened*.

**Osmosis is about water, and the sentence must say so.** *From high to low concentration* is ambiguous at best and wrong at worst, because the **solute** is more concentrated in the direction the **water** is going. Say **water**, say **dilute to concentrated**, and say **partially permeable membrane**. Three parts, three marks.

**Active transport is identified by direction, not by substance.** The same ion can move by diffusion in one place and by active transport in another; what decides it is whether the movement is **with** or **against** the gradient. That is why the root hair example works — the soil is **more dilute** than the cell, so diffusion would empty the cell rather than fill it.

**Two fingerprints of active transport in an unfamiliar question.** Many **mitochondria**, because it needs energy from **respiration**; and uptake that **stops without oxygen** or with a respiratory poison, while diffusion and osmosis carry on. An experiment that switches one process off and leaves another running has told you which was which.

**Percentage change exists because the cylinders differ.** A gain of 0.3 g is **14.999999999999991%** for a 2 g cylinder and **4.9999999999999964%** for a 6 g one — three times the effect, completely hidden by the raw numbers. Dividing by the **original** mass is what makes the comparison honest, and it is the same reasoning as energy per gram in calorimetry.

**Keep the sign, and then say what it means.** Negative means mass was **lost**, so water left, so the solution was **more concentrated** than the cell contents. The number alone earns the calculation mark; the direction earns the biology.

**The cell wall is why plants survive pure water.** An animal cell in pure water **bursts**, because nothing resists the swelling. A plant cell becomes **turgid**: the wall pushes back, and that pressure is what holds a non-woody plant upright. Wilting is the same mechanism in reverse.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Diffusion**: the **net** movement of particles from **high to low** concentration — **down** the gradient. **Passive**.
- Particles never stop moving; at equal concentrations there is simply **no net movement**.
- Diffusion is faster with a **steeper gradient**, a **higher temperature**, a **larger surface area** and a **shorter distance**.
- **Osmosis**: the net movement of **water** from a **dilute** to a **concentrated** solution through a **partially permeable membrane**. **Passive**.
- Partially permeable means **water passes** and the **solute cannot**, so the water has to move instead.
- Plant cell, water in → **turgid**; water out → **flaccid**, then **plasmolysed**.
- Animal cell, water in → may **burst**; water out → **shrinks**. There is **no cell wall** to resist.
- **Active transport**: movement **against** the gradient, using **energy from respiration** and **carrier proteins**.
- Examples: **mineral ions into root hair cells**; **glucose** from the small intestine and the kidney tubules.
- Cells doing a lot of active transport have **many mitochondria**, and their uptake **stops without oxygen**.
- $\% \text{ change} = \dfrac{\text{change}}{\text{original}} \times 100$, keeping the **sign**.
- **Positive** means water moved **in**, so the solution was **more dilute** than the cell.
- **Negative** means water moved **out**, so the solution was **more concentrated**.
- **Core practical 4**: potato cylinders of the same size in sucrose solutions, **blotted dry** the same way, same time and temperature.
- A percentage is used because cylinders do **not start at the same mass**.
- Where the graph **crosses zero**, the solution **matches the cell contents**.

questions.prompt: Compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport, and explain how an experiment could show which process a cell is using to take up a substance.
questions.solution:
**Diffusion** is the **net** movement of particles from a region of **higher** concentration to a region of **lower** concentration — down a **concentration gradient**. It is **passive**: the particles move randomly anyway, and more happen to cross from the crowded side, so no energy from respiration is needed. Oxygen entering a cell is an example.

**Osmosis** is a special case concerning **water**. It is the net movement of **water molecules** from a **dilute** solution to a **concentrated** one, through a **partially permeable membrane**. The membrane is essential: water molecules are small enough to pass but the **solute** is not, so the solute cannot even itself out and the **water** must move instead. Osmosis is also **passive**.

**Active transport** is the opposite case. Substances are moved **against** the concentration gradient, from a **lower** concentration to a **higher** one, which would never happen on its own. It therefore requires **energy from respiration** and **carrier proteins** in the membrane. **Mineral ions entering root hair cells** are the standard example: the soil is far more **dilute** in minerals than the cell already is, so diffusion would move them **out**.

To tell which process a cell is using, exploit the one difference that can be switched off. **Remove the oxygen supply**, or add a respiratory inhibitor such as cyanide, and measure uptake again. **Respiration stops**, so **active transport stops** — but **diffusion and osmosis are passive** and continue unaffected. A substance whose uptake **halts** was being moved actively; one that keeps entering was moving by diffusion or osmosis.

A second, weaker clue points the same way: a cell that does a great deal of active transport needs a great deal of energy, so it contains **many mitochondria**. Root hair cells and the cells lining the small intestine both do.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate the effect of sucrose concentration on potato cylinders, and explain how the results would let you find the concentration inside the potato cells.
questions.solution:
I would cut potato cylinders with a **cork borer**, so that every cylinder has the **same diameter**, and trim them all to the **same length**. Each one is **blotted dry** and its **starting mass** recorded. I would then place one cylinder in each of a range of **sucrose solutions** — for example 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mol/dm³ — using the **same volume** of solution in each tube.

After the **same time**, at the **same temperature**, I would remove each cylinder, **blot it dry in the same way**, and record its **final mass**. The consistency of the blotting matters more than it sounds: surface water left clinging to a cylinder is weighed as though the cells had **absorbed** it, so blotting one harder than another turns a control into a source of error.

For each cylinder I would calculate $\% \text{ change} = \dfrac{\text{change in mass}}{\text{original mass}} \times 100$, keeping the **sign**. A **percentage** is necessary because the cylinders do not all start at the same mass: a gain of 0.3 g is **14.999999999999991%** for a 2 g cylinder but only **4.9999999999999964%** for a 6 g one. Three times as much has happened in the first case, and the raw figures hide that completely.

Plotting **percentage change against concentration** gives a line that falls from positive to negative. Where it **crosses zero** there has been **no net movement of water**, which happens only when the solution outside is at the **same concentration as the cell contents** — so reading that crossing point off the axis gives the concentration inside the potato cells. That is the result of the experiment.

It is worth being precise about what zero means. Water has **not** stopped moving: molecules still cross the membrane in **both** directions, simply at **equal rates**. Above that concentration the solution is more concentrated than the cells, water leaves, and the cylinders **lose** mass; below it, water enters and they **gain**.

criteria.text: Method: cylinders of the same size cut with a cork borer, blotted and weighed, placed in a range of sucrose concentrations.
States control variables: same time, same temperature, same volume of solution, and blotting in the same way.
Calculates percentage change using change ÷ original × 100, and explains why a percentage rather than a raw change.
Explains that where the graph crosses zero there is no net movement, so that concentration equals the cell contents.

questions.modelAnswer:
I would cut potato cylinders with a **cork borer**, so that every cylinder has the **same diameter**, and trim them all to the **same length**. Each one is **blotted dry** and its **starting mass** recorded. I would then place one cylinder in each of a range of **sucrose solutions** — for example 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 mol/dm³ — using the **same volume** of solution in each tube.

After the **same time**, at the **same temperature**, I would remove each cylinder, **blot it dry in the same way**, and record its **final mass**. The consistency of the blotting matters more than it sounds: surface water left clinging to a cylinder is weighed as though the cells had **absorbed** it, so blotting one harder than another turns a control into a source of error.

For each cylinder I would calculate $\% \text{ change} = \dfrac{\text{change in mass}}{\text{original mass}} \times 100$, keeping the **sign**. A **percentage** is necessary because the cylinders do not all start at the same mass: a gain of 0.3 g is **14.999999999999991%** for a 2 g cylinder but only **4.9999999999999964%** for a 6 g one. Three times as much has happened in the first case, and the raw figures hide that completely.

Plotting **percentage change against concentration** gives a line that falls from positive to negative. Where it **crosses zero** there has been **no net movement of water**, which happens only when the solution outside is at the **same concentration as the cell contents** — so reading that crossing point off the axis gives the concentration inside the potato cells. That is the result of the experiment.

It is worth being precise about what zero means. Water has **not** stopped moving: molecules still cross the membrane in **both** directions, simply at **equal rates**. Above that concentration the solution is more concentrated than the cells, water leaves, and the cylinders **lose** mass; below it, water enters and they **gain**.

examTechnique.body:
Three processes, and questions are nearly always asking you to **tell them apart**. Two questions settle it every time: **what moves**, and **which way relative to the gradient**. Water through a partially permeable membrane is **osmosis**; anything else down the gradient is **diffusion**; anything **against** the gradient is **active transport**, and only that one costs energy.

The calculation half is short but strict. Divide by the **original** mass, keep the **sign**, and then say what the sign **means** — the direction of water movement is the biology the number is there to reveal.
examinerErrors: Saying particles **stop moving** when concentrations become equal, rather than that there is **no net movement**.
Defining osmosis as movement *from high to low concentration* without saying it is the **water** that moves.
Leaving **partially permeable membrane** out of the osmosis definition.
Calling something active transport because of **what** moves rather than **which way** it moves.
Dividing by the **final** mass instead of the **original** mass in the percentage calculation.
Dropping the **minus sign**, so a loss of mass is reported as a gain.
Saying a plant cell in pure water **bursts** — the **cell wall** makes it **turgid** instead.
Forgetting to **blot** the cylinders, or not blotting them all the same way.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer gives the osmosis definition in its **three** parts — **water**, **dilute to concentrated**, **partially permeable membrane** — without needing to be prompted for the third. It uses the word **net** deliberately, and can explain that a cylinder with no mass change has water crossing **both ways at equal rates**, which is what makes the graph's zero crossing meaningful. It identifies active transport by **direction**, not by substance, and knows the two fingerprints: **many mitochondria**, and uptake that **stops without oxygen** while osmosis carries on. In the calculation it divides by the **original** mass, keeps the sign, and finishes by saying which way the water moved and what that says about the solution.
